title: The Christmas Interpreter: from the Kruislaan to the Transfer of Power
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: The Hague, the last day of January
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In The Hague, on the last day of January 1956, Guido van Rossum is born. The sources give the city and the date and then stop. No hospital is named, and no street, so the pin sits on the city centre by default. A younger brother, Just, follows him into the world and into an adjacent craft. Just becomes a type designer, and the letters of the Python Powered logo, carried on stickers and conference badges through four decades of the language's life, are drawn by his hand and not by Guido's.
suggested_refs: Birth records of the municipality of The Hague, January 1956

stops.name: Haarlem, the boyhood city
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: Dutch Wikipedia places his upbringing in Haarlem but names neither the year of the move nor the school; the date is a placeholder inside the schooling years
stops.campa: The family lives in Haarlem, fifteen kilometres west of Amsterdam, and there the boy is schooled. Which school, the reachable sources decline to say, and the year the family arrives from The Hague goes unrecorded too. What survives of the childhood is a shape rather than a record: a Dutch provincial town within a bicycle ride of the university and the computing centre that will hold him for the next twenty years. He does not leave this small corner of the country until he is nearly forty, and the language he is known for is written inside it.
suggested_refs: Haarlem secondary school registers of the late 1960s, unidentified in reachable sources

stops.name: Haarlem, the youth league for nature study
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the membership is attested, the years are not
stops.campa: As a teenager he is active in the Nederlandse Jeugdbond voor Natuurstudie, the Dutch youth league for nature study, an organisation run by its own adolescents rather than by adults, whose discipline is field observation: name the thing, record where you found it, do not report what you did not see. The sources that document his life give the membership and no dates, neither the year he joins nor the year he leaves. It is the earliest institution he joins that is not a school.
suggested_refs: Archives of the Nederlandse Jeugdbond voor Natuurstudie (NJN)

stops.name: Erfurt, bronze at the Olympiad
stops.date_confidence: attested for the medal and the year; the July dating follows the IMO's published schedule for the Erfurt olympiad
stops.campa: He crosses a border for the first time in the record, into East Germany, to sit the International Mathematical Olympiad for the Netherlands, and comes home with a bronze medal. Wikipedia attests the medal and the year; the venue, Erfurt, is drawn from the olympiad's own published host history rather than from any biography of him. The mathematics that wins it is the ordinary competition kind: problems with answers. Nothing in the trip predicts a language, and the sources make no such claim on its behalf.
suggested_refs: Official results archive of the 16th International Mathematical Olympiad, Erfurt, 1974

stops.name: Roeterseiland, the university enrolment
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the 1982 degree is attested, the 1974 matriculation is an inference from it; no source states the year he began
stops.campa: He enrols at the University of Amsterdam to read mathematics and computer science. The teaching sits on the Roeterseiland campus, a block of concrete faculties on an island in the ring of canals east of the centre. The pool's original coordinate for this stop fell a kilometre southeast on the Amsteldijk and has been corrected to Roetersstraat. The starting year is not attested anywhere reachable: it is worked backwards from the degree of 1982, and is recorded here as an inference rather than a fact.
suggested_refs: University of Amsterdam student registers, Faculty of Mathematics, 1974-1982

stops.name: SARA on the Kruislaan, the student systems programmer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by his own resume; the month is not given
stops.campa: Still a student, he takes part-time work as a systems programmer at SARA, the Stichting Academisch Rekencentrum Amsterdam, the academic computing centre out on the Kruislaan in the eastern suburbs. The address decides the rest of his life. SARA stands on the same road as the Mathematical Centre, and he will work for the next eighteen years within a few hundred metres of this door. He learns the machine from the operator's side first, mounting the tapes and answering the users who file complaints against the queue.
suggested_refs: SARA (Stichting Academisch Rekencentrum Amsterdam), Kruislaan, personnel records 1977-1982

stops.name: Roeterseiland, the master's degree
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded in any reachable source, and defaults to January
stops.campa: He takes his master's degree in mathematics and computer science from the University of Amsterdam. It is the last academic credential he will hold. No doctorate follows, and none is ever sought: the man who will be called the benevolent dictator of a language taught to first-year students in dozens of countries holds a single Dutch master's and nothing above it. He walks out of the Roeterseiland faculty and, in the same year, across the city to the Mathematical Centre on the Kruislaan, where the language begins.
suggested_refs: University of Amsterdam degree records, 1982

stops.name: CWI, Kruislaan 413: the ABC group
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by his own resume, which gives the period 1982-1986
stops.campa: He joins the Centrum Wiskunde en Informatica at Kruislaan 413 and is put on ABC, a teaching language built to be learned by people who are not programmers. ABC marks its blocks by indentation rather than by braces, on the reasoning that the eye already reads the indentation, which leaves the braces as a redundant second statement of the same thing, and one that can contradict it. He works on its design and implementation for four years. Python will inherit that decision entire, and be argued about for it ever after.
stops.quote: I decided to design a language of my own which would borrow everything I liked from ABC while at the same time fixing all its problems (as I perceived them).
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com, January 2009
suggested_refs: The ABC programming language reports and implementation, CWI, 1982-1986

stops.name: CWI, the Amoeba project and a routine called glob
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; his resume gives the period 1986-1991
stops.campa: He moves within the building onto Amoeba, a distributed operating system that treats a room full of machines as one computer. The same year, a small routine of his for expanding filename patterns, glob, is taken into BSD Unix and from there into the general inheritance of the system; it is his first code to travel further than the institute. Amoeba needs a language above C for stitching its services together, and has none. Three years later, over a holiday, he stops waiting for one.
stops.quote: My original motivation for creating Python was the perceived need for a higher level language in the Amoeba project.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com, January 2009
suggested_refs: The Amoeba distributed operating system papers, CWI and Vrije Universiteit, 1986-1991

stops.name: CWI, the two-week holiday
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; he places the start in late December 1989 and describes it as a two-week Christmas holiday, without naming a day
stops.campa: The institute closes for Christmas. He has two weeks and nothing scheduled, and he does not want to log in to the CWI machines to fill them, so he writes the first pieces of an interpreter on the Macintosh at home. It keeps what he liked in ABC, the indentation and the high-level types, and drops what he did not: a closed system that refuses extension because it assumes its user will be a beginner forever. By the first months of 1990 the thing runs.
stops.quote: I had a two-week Christmas holiday with nothing to do. So, I wrote the first bits of the Python interpreter on my Mac so that I didn't have to log into CWI's computers.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, interview, Linux Journal, 1998
suggested_refs: The earliest surviving CWI-era Python sources, reconstructed in the python/cpython history repository
sources: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com, January 2009

stops.name: CWI, the name off the television
stops.date_confidence: inferred: van Rossum places the naming at the start of the project, but gives no date for it
stops.campa: The thing needs a name and he does not deliberate. He is reading the scripts of Monty Python's Flying Circus at the time and takes the first thing that comes to mind. The snake is nobody's idea: it arrives later, from readers who assume a herpetological seriousness the author never had, and by the time the misunderstanding is general it is also permanent. The language is named after a BBC comedy troupe by a Dutch researcher on a holiday, and the joke is never retracted.
stops.quote: I picked the first thing that came to mind, which happened to be Monty Python's Flying Circus, one of my favorite comedy troupes.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com, January 2009
suggested_refs: Monty Python's Flying Circus scripts, BBC, 1969-1974
sources: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com

stops.name: CWI, posted to alt.sources
stops.date_confidence: attested: van Rossum's own brief timeline of Python gives 20 February 1991 for 0.9.0; note that Wikipedia's 'History of Python' reports the first public version as 0.9.1, a contradiction left standing here
stops.campa: Fourteen months after the holiday he posts the interpreter to the Usenet newsgroup alt.sources, where anyone may take it. His own timeline records the release as 0.9.0 on 20 February 1991; Wikipedia's history of the language reports 0.9.1 instead, and the two accounts are not reconciled by any source reachable for this file. There is no licence negotiation and no institutional release process, and the announcement is the post itself. It goes out of the building the way source code went out of buildings in 1991.
stops.quote: So, like almost everything I've written, Python was open source before the term was even invented by Eric Raymond and Bruce Perens in late 1997.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Personal History, Part 1: CWI,' python-history.blogspot.com, January 2009
suggested_refs: The February 1991 alt.sources posting of Python 0.9.0, Usenet archives
sources: Guido van Rossum, 'A Brief Timeline of Python'

stops.name: CWI, the multimedia group
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; his resume gives the period 1991-1995
stops.campa: Inside CWI he moves again, from Amoeba to the multimedia group, working on hypermedia systems and the synchronisation of streams across a network. Python is not his job. It is the thing he does beside the job, in an institute that permits it, and the arrangement will repeat itself at every employer he has for the next thirty years: the language is always adjacent to the work he is paid for, and always outlives it. The multimedia work ends in 1995 when he leaves the country. The language does not.
suggested_refs: CWI multimedia group publications, 1991-1995

stops.name: CWI, Python 1.0
stops.date_confidence: attested: van Rossum's own timeline gives 26 January 1994; the research pool placed this release in the USA, which is wrong, since he did not leave the Netherlands until April 1995
stops.campa: Python reaches 1.0 on 26 January 1994, and it is released from Amsterdam, not from America: he is still at CWI and will be for another fourteen months. The version brings the functional tools, lambda, map, filter and reduce, into a language whose author is not himself a partisan of that style and who will spend years afterward trying to talk users out of the worst of it. A holiday project has acquired a version one, and with it a public that expects a version two on some schedule other than his own.
stops.quote: extensibility was important from the start with Python, and it's not difficult to write an extension to interface to a new C library.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, interview, Linux Journal, 1998
suggested_refs: Python 1.0.0 release announcement, January 1994
sources: Guido van Rossum, 'A Brief Timeline of Python'

stops.name: Gaithersburg, guest at the Bureau of Standards
stops.date_confidence: attested: his resume gives mid-October to mid-December 1994; the research pool had dated this stint 'c. 1995', which is wrong
stops.campa: For two months at the end of 1994 he is a guest researcher at the National Institute of Standards and Technology in Gaithersburg, Maryland, on the far side of the Atlantic from every previous address in this journey. It is the first American footing, temporary and paid for by the agency that houses it. He continues Python work there. Then he goes home to Amsterdam for the winter, and returns in the spring for good, to a different state and a different institution, on money from this same agency.
suggested_refs: NIST guest researcher records, Gaithersburg, October-December 1994

stops.name: Reston, the Corporation for National Research Initiatives
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by his own resume, which gives April 1995 to February 1998 as a NIST-funded guest researcher based at CNRI
stops.campa: He crosses for good in April 1995 to Reston, Virginia, and to the Corporation for National Research Initiatives, which Bob Kahn founded here in 1986 and still chairs. The atlas already holds this address under Kahn's name, and the coordinate is inherited from his file unchanged. Van Rossum arrives not as a CNRI employee but as a guest researcher on NIST money, working on mobile agents and distributed systems; the employment becomes direct only in March 1998. Vint Cerf's own CNRI years run through the same corridor.
suggested_refs: CNRI, 1895 Preston White Drive, Reston, Virginia; personnel and project records 1995-2000
sources: vint_cerf.journey.json, stop 'Reston, back with Kahn at CNRI'

stops.name: Reston, Grail: a browser written in Python
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: Grail began August 1995 with a first public release that November, and ran to version 0.6 in 1999; the research pool's 'c. 1996-1999' range is corrected here
stops.campa: At CNRI he leads Grail, a web browser written entirely in Python, begun in August 1995 and first released in November of that year. It is a demonstration as much as a product, proof that a language posted to a newsgroup six years earlier can carry an application the size of a browser. Grail reaches 0.6 in 1999 and stops. The browsers that survive are written in C, and the language Grail was built to prove goes on to be used for nearly everything except browsers.
suggested_refs: The Grail browser source distribution, CNRI, 1995-1999

stops.name: Reston, the meeting that names the dictator
stops.date_confidence: attested to the meeting by van Rossum's own later reconstruction of the term's origin; he traces it to a Python meeting in 1995 and dates it 18 April, while noting the coinage was never formally recorded
stops.campa: At a Python workshop the community fixes on a title for him: Benevolent Dictator For Life. It is given, not taken. He does not adopt it; he is handed it by the people who have decided to accept his final say on the design, and he spends years afterward correcting the folklore that grows around it, including the claim that it comes from a Monty Python sketch. The title lasts more than two decades and describes an arrangement no charter ever wrote down: one man decides, and the argument stops.
stops.quote: I believe I've tracked down the origin of the term Benevolent Dictator For Life (BDFL) to a Python meeting in 1995.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Origin of BDFL,' Artima weblog, 31 July 2008
suggested_refs: Van Rossum's Artima weblog post 'Origin of BDFL,' 31 July 2008
sources: Guido van Rossum, Artima weblog, 'The BDFL' / 'Origin of BDFL', 2008

stops.name: Reston, Python 1.5 and a payroll
stops.date_confidence: attested: van Rossum's timeline gives 3 January 1998 for Python 1.5; the research pool dated it December 1997, which is wrong
stops.campa: Python 1.5 goes out on 3 January 1998, and two months later he stops being a guest and becomes an employee of CNRI outright. The institution around him is Kahn's, and its habits are the habits of the request-for-comments culture that Kahn and Cerf built: proposals circulated in plain text, numbered, argued in public, adopted or dropped on the record. The Python Enhancement Proposal will be that machinery narrowed to one language, and the debt is one van Rossum has stated himself.
suggested_refs: Python 1.5 release notes, January 1998; the PEP process as descendant of the IETF RFC series
sources: Guido van Rossum, 'A Brief Timeline of Python'

stops.name: Fremont, the startup that lasts five months
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the move; the Fremont office location is a reconstruction and is not independently confirmed
stops.campa: He leaves CNRI with three other core developers for BeOpen.com, where he directs a unit called PythonLabs. The company is a creature of the moment: open source has become an asset class, and a team that maintains a widely used language is a thing an investor will pay for. The office pin here is reconstructed rather than attested. Five months later the company is gone, and the four men who moved together look for a new employer with the language intact and nothing else to show for the year.
suggested_refs: BeOpen.com corporate records, 2000

stops.name: Fremont, Python 2.0
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month only; the day is not recorded in the pool, and the office coordinate is inherited from the reconstructed BeOpen pin
stops.campa: Python 2.0 is released in October 2000, carrying list comprehensions and a garbage collector that can detect reference cycles, which is to say a language that now cleans up after structures pointing at themselves. It ships from a company in the act of failing. The release is not delayed for that. The pattern is established and will hold for twenty years: the corporate custodian changes, and the release numbers advance on their own schedule regardless of who is paying the rent that month.
suggested_refs: Python 2.0 release announcement, October 2000

stops.name: Fredericksburg, PythonLabs at Zope
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; his resume gives October 2000 to July 2003
stops.campa: BeOpen collapses and the whole of PythonLabs moves intact to Zope Corporation in Fredericksburg, Virginia, with van Rossum still directing it. The team has now been transferred between three employers in six months and has lost no one. What is being moved from company to company is not a product line but a small group of people who know how the interpreter works. No foundation holds the language yet, and each of these employers takes custody of it by hiring the men who write it.
suggested_refs: Zope Corporation, Fredericksburg, Virginia; PythonLabs 2000-2003

stops.name: Wilmington, the Foundation takes title
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of incorporation; the month is not recorded in the pool and defaults to January
stops.campa: The Python Software Foundation is incorporated to hold the language's intellectual property, with van Rossum among its founders, and the run of corporate custodians ends: no company owns Python again. In the same year the Free Software Foundation gives him its Award for the Advancement of Free Software, presented in 2002 for the year 2001. The legal question of who owns the thing is now closed. The political question of who decides it remains open, and is answered by one name for another seventeen years.
suggested_refs: Python Software Foundation certificate of incorporation, Delaware, 2001

stops.name: Washington, the first PyCon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the exact days of the first PyCon are not recorded in the pool
stops.campa: Two hundred people gather in Washington for the first PyCon. Thirteen years after a Dutch researcher wrote an interpreter on a home Macintosh to fill a holiday, the users of the thing convene in a room and can see each other. The conference series will spread to other countries and carry, in each of them, a national suffix. Van Rossum attends this first one as what he already is at these events and will remain long after resigning the title: the person the room turns toward when a decision has to be made.
suggested_refs: Proceedings and programme of PyCon 2003, Washington, D.C.

stops.name: San Mateo, the security language
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month by his resume, which gives July 2003 to December 2005; the San Mateo office coordinate is reconstructed to the town rather than to an address
stops.campa: He leaves Zope for Elemental Security as senior language architect, and designs a custom language in which a company can state its security policy. It is the one stretch of his career whose product is invisible outside the firm that bought it. Two and a half years produce one proprietary language and no public release. The Python work continues beside it, unpaid and unmanaged, as it has beside every job since Amoeba, and by December 2005 an employer appears who is willing to pay for that part directly.
suggested_refs: Elemental Security, San Mateo, California, product and personnel records 2003-2005

stops.name: Mountain View, half his hours for the language
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; his resume gives December 2005 to December 2012
stops.campa: Google hires him in December 2005 and grants him what no previous employer did: a portion of his working week for Python itself, paid. He builds Mondrian, an internal code review tool, which is later rewritten outside the company as Rietveld. Vint Cerf joined the same firm two months earlier as its Chief Internet Evangelist, working from Reston rather than the Californian campus, and the atlas's Googleplex coordinate is inherited from Cerf's file unchanged. No source says the two men ever met here.
suggested_refs: Mondrian and Rietveld code review tools, Google, 2006-2008
sources: vint_cerf.journey.json, stop 'Mountain View, the title he invents for himself'

stops.name: Mountain View, named Distinguished Engineer
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded in the pool and defaults to January
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery names him a Distinguished Engineer. It is the first of the professional honours, and it arrives from the discipline's own bureaucracy rather than from the free software world that gave him the previous one. The list will lengthen: a fellowship of the Computer History Museum, a Dijkstra fellowship from the institute on the Kruislaan, a Japanese prize for information technology. None of them changes the arrangement by which Python is governed, which is still that he decides.
suggested_refs: ACM Distinguished Engineer citations, 2006

stops.name: Mountain View, App Engine
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by his resume; the month is not given
stops.campa: Inside Google he works on App Engine, the platform that lets an outside developer run code on the company's machines, and on its data layer: the NDB datastore library, the Appstats profiling tool. App Engine launches supporting exactly one language, and it is his. A platform built by the largest advertising company on earth accepts, as its first and for a while its only tongue, the interpreter a researcher wrote on a Macintosh over Christmas because his institute's computers were inconvenient to log in to.
suggested_refs: Google App Engine launch documentation, 2008; the NDB datastore library

stops.name: Mountain View, Python 3.0 and the break
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the pool does not supply the day
stops.campa: Python 3.0 is released in December 2008 under his direction, and it does not run the previous version's programs. The break is deliberate: accumulated errors in the language are corrected all at once, on the reasoning that a decade of half-measures is worse than one clean cut. Support for the old version is not withdrawn until 2020. The migration occupies the language's users for twelve years, and the man who ordered it spends a good part of the next decade at a company doing that work by hand.
suggested_refs: Python 3.0 release announcement and the 2to3 migration tooling, December 2008

stops.name: Mountain View, the seventh year ends
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On 7 December 2012 he leaves Google after seven years. It is the longest stretch he has spent at any employer since CWI, and the only one at which developing Python was written into the job rather than done beside it. He is fifty-six. The language is twenty-three and is by now taught to first-year students on four continents, and its author is once again between companies, carrying with him nothing that belongs to Google and everything that belongs to a foundation incorporated in Delaware.
suggested_refs: Van Rossum's public departure announcement from Google, December 2012

stops.name: Berry Street, joining Dropbox
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the pin is set on Dropbox's 2013 address at 185 Berry Street, correcting a pool coordinate that fell near Rincon Hill on no Dropbox site at all
stops.campa: In January 2013 he joins Dropbox, whose service is built on Python and whose codebase has grown past the size at which a language without declared types is comfortable. He begins work on mypy, a static type checker that reads annotations and finds the errors a compiler would have found. The company moves offices twice during his tenure, to Brannan Street in 2014 and to Mission Bay in 2019, and the pins in this segment follow the buildings rather than a single fixed headquarters.
suggested_refs: Dropbox, 185 Berry Street, San Francisco, 2013; the mypy project repository

stops.name: Brannan Street, PEP 484
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of acceptance; the pin is set on Dropbox's Brannan Street offices, the company's address in 2015, rather than on any location the PEP itself names
stops.campa: PEP 484 is accepted, and Python acquires optional static type hints: annotations that the interpreter ignores at runtime and that a separate checker reads. He authors it and shepherds it through. The design is a compromise with the language's own history, since twenty-five years of Python was written without types and none of it is required to change. What was a research question in the ABC group in 1982, how much structure to demand from a writer before running their program, is answered here as a choice offered rather than a rule imposed.
stops.quote: code is read much more often than it is written
stops.quote_source: PEP 8, Style Guide for Python Code (Guido van Rossum, Barry Warsaw, Nick Coghlan)
suggested_refs: PEP 484, Type Hints, peps.python.org

stops.name: Brannan Street, four million lines
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the annotation effort spans his Dropbox years and no single date marks it; the pool's claim that he directed a five-million-line Python 2 migration is not supported and is corrected here
stops.campa: Dropbox annotates its back-end Python with types until nearly four million lines are statically checked, the largest such body of code then known. The separate migration of the application from Python 2 to Python 3, over a million lines, is led by other engineers, who name van Rossum in their acknowledgements and not among the authors of the work. The distinction matters and the popular account erases it. He builds the instrument. Other people, at this company and at thousands of others, do the migration with it.
suggested_refs: Dropbox engineering blog posts on the Python 3 migration and on type checking at scale

stops.name: Belmont, the transfer of power
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the mailing-list post; the physical location is a reconstruction from his known Bay Area residence, since nothing places him at home when he wrote it
stops.campa: On 12 July 2018, after a bitter fight over PEP 572 and the assignment expression it added, he writes to the python-committers list that he is done. He appoints no successor and proposes no structure, and he asks the developers, in the post's own words, what they intend to do now: a democracy, an anarchy, a dictatorship, a federation. Twenty-three years of one man deciding end in an email of a few hundred words, and the community is told to work out its own government.
stops.quote: Now that PEP 572 is done, I don't ever want to have to fight so hard for a PEP and find that so many people despise my decisions.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Transfer of Power,' python-committers mailing list, 12 July 2018
suggested_refs: The 'Transfer of Power' post, python-committers archives, 12 July 2018; PEP 572

stops.name: Mountain View, Fellow of the Computer History Museum
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only; the month is not recorded, and the coordinate is set on the museum's Shoreline Boulevard address, which the research pool did not supply
stops.campa: The Computer History Museum makes him a Fellow for the invention of Python, in the same calendar year he resigns the leadership of it. The institution that collects the machines has decided the language belongs in the collection, and its author is enrolled among the people the field has finished arguing about. He is sixty-two and neither retired nor in charge: the museum honours a completed thing while the thing itself continues to release twice a year under a governance that does not yet exist.
suggested_refs: Computer History Museum Fellow Awards, 2018, Mountain View, California

stops.name: Belmont, elected to the Council he made necessary
stops.date_confidence: attested: PEP 8100 records nominations from 7 to 20 January 2019 and voting from 21 January to 4 February; the research pool's 'January 2019' is corrected here, and the pin is a residence rather than a place, since the election was electronic
stops.campa: The core developers elect a five-member Steering Council, and he is among the five, with Barry Warsaw, Brett Cannon, Carol Willing and Alyssa Coghlan. The man who refused to name a successor is returned to office as one vote in five by the people he told to invent a government. The vote is electronic and has no address, and the pin here is his house for want of a room to put it in. He serves a single term and then, in 2020, withdraws his name from the ballot and does not stand again.
stops.quote: I am not going to appoint a successor.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Transfer of Power,' python-committers mailing list, 12 July 2018
suggested_refs: PEP 8100, the 2019 Python Steering Council election results

stops.name: Kruislaan, a fellowship from the old institute
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not recorded in the pool and defaults to January
stops.campa: CWI names him a Dijkstra Fellow, after the Dutchman who worked in this same institute and who argued all his life for programs whose correctness could be proved rather than tested. The Netherlands has honoured him twice now, having given him the NLUUG award in May 2003. Thirty-seven years after he walked in from the university to work on a teaching language nobody outside the building used, the building calls him back to name a fellowship after him and hand it to him.
suggested_refs: CWI Dijkstra Fellowship citations, 2019; NLUUG award, May 2003

stops.name: Mission Bay, retiring from Dropbox
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month only; his resume gives October 2019 with no day, and the pin follows Dropbox's 2019 address at 1800 Owens Street
stops.campa: In October 2019 he retires from Dropbox and from employment altogether, at sixty-three. Six years of type checking end without a farewell tour. The permanent vacation he announced in 2018 was from the office of Benevolent Dictator and not from work; this is the other one, the ordinary kind, and it lasts about twelve months. The accounts that merge the two events, and put the permanent vacation phrase in his mouth here, are conflating a resignation with a retirement a year and a quarter apart.
stops.quote: I'm tired, and need a very long break.
stops.quote_source: Guido van Rossum, 'Transfer of Power,' python-committers mailing list, 12 July 2018

stops.name: Belmont, the year off

stops.name: Belmont, no tomb
stops.date_confidence: current as of the sources consulted in August 2026; this stop records a living person and has no terminal date
stops.campa: There is no grave and no monument to record, and no fate of a tomb: he is alive, retired, and living in Belmont, California. The atlas notes this as a gap it declines to fill. What stands in place of a tomb is the interpreter, and a document he did not write: the Zen of Python, nineteen aphorisms printed by typing import this, composed by Tim Peters and attributed by nearly everyone to Guido. The best-known legend about the man is therefore a legend about sentences somebody else wrote.
stops.quote: Beautiful is better than ugly. Explicit is better than implicit. Simple is better than complex.
